<div class="adr-inshort"><span class="adr-inshort-label">In short</span><p>where a name's <em>spelling</em> and its <em>resolution</em> can come apart, Novis refuses the input rather than repairing it — never normalising, unfolding, mangling or truncating its way to an interpretation. <a class="adr-source-link" href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/docs/adr/0095-ambiguous-input-is-refused-never-repaired.md">View the source of this decision on GitHub</a>

## Context

PHP's security record from 2023 to 2026 has one shape in it more often than any other, and it is not a
memory bug. It is a parser that, given text it cannot read unambiguously, **repairs the text and carries
on**:

| PHP fixed | What was repaired instead of refused |
|---|---|
| CVE-2025-1217 | an `obs-fold` continuation line was unfolded and parsed |
| CVE-2025-1734 | a header line with no colon was treated as a header |
| CVE-2025-1736 | a header check omitted the basic-auth header |
| CVE-2025-1861 | a redirect `Location` longer than 1024 bytes was truncated and followed |
| CVE-2025-1219 | a redirected resource's charset was read from the wrong `Content-Type` |
| CVE-2025-1220 | a hostname containing NUL was accepted |
| CVE-2024-11234 | CR/LF in a proxy URI reached the wire |
| CVE-2022-31629, then CVE-2024-2756 | `$_COOKIE` key mangling (`.` and space to `_`) made a plain cookie readable as a `__Host-` one — the second CVE is the incomplete fix for the first |
| CVE-2023-0662 | a body under every size cap held enough multipart parts to exhaust the filesystem |

The same shape produces the Windows half. A path component's spelling and its resolution come apart there
by design: `foo.` opens `foo`, `CON` is a device in every directory, `file.txt::$DATA` opens the default
stream, and `PROGRA~1` aliases a long name. A component can pass a lexical containment check and resolve
outside the base.

One argument says this is Novis's problem rather than a deployment's, and a proxy in front makes it stronger
rather than weaker.

**"A proxy does it earlier and better" is true for limits and false for parsing.** Request smuggling *is* a
proxy/origin parser differential: it exists precisely because two parsers read one byte stream differently.
Delegating leniency to the proxy is not a mitigation, it is the mechanism. [0074](/docs/adr/0074/)
drew that line for size and rate, where it is correct, and the wording did not distinguish the two.

**A production deployment always has a proxy in front of it**
([0097](/docs/adr/0097/) § 1), which is exactly the deployment a lenient
origin parser is dangerous in — the differential needs two parsers to exist, and there they both are.

## Decision

**Where a name's spelling and its resolution can differ, Novis refuses the input. It never normalises,
mangles, truncates or unfolds its way to an interpretation.**

### 1. Two classes, and only the first refuses

An input is **ambiguous** when two conforming readers can disagree about what it says. An input is merely
**unusual** when every reader agrees and the spelling is only uncommon.

- **Ambiguous → refuse the whole message or operation**, with a diagnostic naming the defect. Never a
  partial read, never a repair.
- **Unusual → accept verbatim.** No renaming, no case folding, no truncation, no substitution.

The ambiguity list is **closed and written down** — §§ 2, 3, 4 and 5 are all of it. That is what makes the
rule testable and fuzzable, and it is what stops "strict" from growing every time somebody reads a
specification more carefully. A defect not on the list is accepted; adding one is an amendment to this ADR.

### 2. The closed list, for an HTTP message

Refused, on a request Novis receives **and on a response Novis's outbound client receives**:

| Defect | Why it is ambiguous |
|---|---|
| an `obs-fold` continuation line | RFC 9110 requires a server to reject or replace it; two readers differ on where the value ends |
| a header line with no colon | it is not a header, and treating it as one invents a name |
| CTL, NUL, CR or LF anywhere in a header name or value | the framing itself becomes reader-dependent |
| duplicate `Content-Length` | two answers to how long the body is |
| `Content-Length` together with `Transfer-Encoding` | the classic smuggling pair |
| NUL anywhere in a hostname | the name resolved is not the name written |
| a `Location`, hostname or URI longer than its configured maximum | truncating produces a *different, valid* value, which is worse than an error |
| a request path containing a dot-segment or an encoded separator (`%2f`) | the path a mount is selected by and the path a reader sees come apart ([0097](/docs/adr/0097/) § 6) |
| an `X-Forwarded-For` token in the trusted-walk position that neither names an address nor withholds one | the value was about to be used as the client's address and cannot be read as one; a token that *withholds* it — `unknown` — has said something definite and is not refused ([0097](/docs/adr/0097/) § 6) |

**No opt-out on the outbound half.** A remote server is an attacker — php-src CVE-2024-8929 had a hostile
MySQL server read one client's heap containing another user's query — and a response's body flows straight
into program logic. An upstream emitting genuinely ambiguous headers is one whose answers cannot be
reasoned about, and a throw at the call site is the honest outcome.

### 3. A cookie name is bytes, and a prefix has one meaning

`Core\Request::cookie(name)` matches **byte for byte**. No character is substituted, in either direction.
PHP's dot-and-space mangling existed for `register_globals`-era variable names, and
[0012](/docs/adr/0012/) deleted the superglobals it served.

The runtime enforces the prefixes rather than documenting them:

- `__Host-` requires `Secure`, requires `Path=/`, and forbids `Domain`.
- `__Secure-` requires `Secure`.

A non-conforming cookie carrying either prefix is **not visible** to the program on read, and is refused on
write. A prefix whose meaning depends on every read site checking it is the arrangement that produced
CVE-2024-2756; enforcing it once, in the one place that parses the header, is the whole fix.

### 4. Multipart caps a part count, not only a body size

`[limits] max_multipart_parts` (default **1000**, PHP's own number after CVE-2023-0662), plus a per-part
field-name length and a per-part size, all `nvs.toml` directives per [0064](/docs/adr/0064/).
Exceeding any is a `413` naming the limit and the directive.

The body-size cap [0074](/docs/adr/0074/) already keeps is not this: the cost of a
part is bookkeeping and a temp file, not bytes, so a body well inside every size cap can still exhaust
inodes. This also widens [0004](/docs/adr/0004/)'s attribution rule in the only direction it
was missing — **temp files, file descriptors and disk bytes are charged to a request the same way memory
is.**

### 5. A path component that does not spell what it resolves to

`Core\IO::within` — the launderer, and the one place the base directory is known — refuses a component
that:

- is a Windows reserved device name (`CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `COM1`–`COM9`, `LPT1`–`LPT9`), with or
  without an extension;
- ends in a dot or a space;
- contains a colon;
- matches the 8.3 short-name pattern (`NAME~digit`).

**On every platform, not only Windows.** A rule that fires on one host and not another means a suite that
passes in CI fails in production, and the developer writing the check is usually on the host where it
silently does nothing. This repository runs conformance on a native Windows leg *and* a WSL leg, so a
platform-conditional answer would need two expectations for one member.

`Core\Path` is untouched by all of this. It stays pure string algebra, it touches no disk, it carries no
policy, and it goes on accepting `/` and `\` as separators on every platform —
`crates/nvs-stdlib/src/path.rs`'s own module doc owns why, and the reason is the two legs above.
`Path::normalize` is still **not** a launderer, because the base is not part of its input.

## Consequences

- **A client that sends `obs-fold` cannot talk to Novis.** It was deprecated in 2014 and RFC 9110 requires
  a server to reject or replace it; this picks reject.
- **An upstream with a sloppy header emitter breaks an outbound call**, visibly, at the call site. This is
  the cost the § 2 note argues is worth paying, and it is the one entry in this ADR most likely to be
  reported as a bug.
- **A form with more than 1000 parts needs one config line.** Matching PHP's post-CVE default means a
  ported application meets the limit exactly where it already met one.
- **A POSIX file named `foo.` or `a:b` is unreachable *through the launderer*.** It remains reachable by an
  absolute path the program supplies itself, which is not laundered and never was.
- **Strict parsing is not slower.** Validation folds into the pass that already touches every byte to find
  delimiters; it is *lenient* parsing that needs extra work to unfold, re-scan and normalise. Measured
  basis: byte-class validation of a 600–900 byte header block is ≈230 ns worst case, ≈0.002% of a 10 ms
  request.

## Alternatives rejected

- **Normalise and continue, as PHP does.** Maximum interoperability, and the posture that produced every
  row of the *Context* table. It also guarantees that Novis and any proxy in front of it can disagree about
  what a request says.
- **Total strictness — refuse anything not conforming to RFC 9110's grammar.** Stronger and simpler to
  state, and it rejects requests every other origin accepts (underscores in header names are common). It
  also makes the rule open-ended, which is exactly what § 1's closed list exists to prevent.
- **A per-call opt-out on the outbound half.** Buys integration with sloppy third-party APIs, which is a
  real problem. Rejected because the second code path must be kept exactly as safe as the first, and an
  option like that is copy-pasted into the calls that did not need it.
- **Leave prefix enforcement to the program, with a `Core\Cookie` helper.** This is precisely PHP's
  arrangement: the prefix means nothing unless every read site checks it, and CVE-2024-2756 exists because
  one site did not.
- **A PHP-compatibility mode reproducing cookie-name mangling.** Rejected: the mangling *is* the bypass,
  and [0080](/docs/adr/0080/) makes PHP syntax an on-ramp rather than a compatibility
  promise.
- **Enforce the § 5 refusals only on Windows.** Rejected in § 5: a platform-conditional security rule is
  tested on the platform where it does nothing.
- **Put the § 5 refusals in `Core\Path::normalize`.** Rejected: spec § 8's premise is that no `Path` member
  carries policy, and putting policy there invites the belief that normalising is safe. Containment needs
  the base, and only `IO::within` has it.

## Verification

- A `.nvst` case per row of § 2's table, on the inbound parser and on the outbound client, asserting the
  message is refused whole and the diagnostic names the defect.
- A case asserting a header name containing an underscore, and one containing an unknown-but-well-formed
  name, are both accepted **verbatim** — the *unusual* half of § 1, which is as much of the rule as the
  refusals.
- A case asserting `Core\Request::cookie("a.b")` reads a cookie named `a.b`, and that a `__Host-` cookie
  without `Secure` is invisible on read and refused on write.
- A multipart fixture at 1000 and at 1001 parts, and one whose body is far under the size cap while its
  part count is far over it.
- A `Core\IO::within` case per § 5 bullet, running on **both** legs and expecting the same answer.
- A fuzz target on the HTTP message parser, beside `fuzz/fuzz_targets/lex.rs` and `parse.rs`, whose
  invariant is that no input produces a partial or repaired read: every input either parses whole or is
  refused.
